extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduates or graduate students learning foundations of algebraic geometry (readers of Ravi Vakil's notes)
extracted.subtask_description: Definitions, constructions, and key properties for projective schemes: graded rings, the Proj construction, the topology and structure sheaf on Proj, and several worked examples (A2−{0}, doubled origin, Pn, cones, CRT interpretation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of a function at a point via residue field
rubrics_metrics.description: The value of a function at a point p is its image in the residue field κ(p) (i.e., reduce the function modulo the prime corresponding to p and interpret in the residue field). For the generic point of an irreducible closed subset, the value lies in the fraction field of the coordinate ring of that component.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: compute (x(y^2 − x^5))^{-1} at (2,4) by reducing to the residue field; value at the generic point of the x-axis by setting y=0 gives an element of k(x). Check computations if they seem mysterious. Use explicit examples (e.g., 27/4 on Spec Z minus primes) to build intuition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fiber of an OX-module at a point
rubrics_metrics.description: Definition: If F is an OX-module on a scheme X, the fiber of F at p ∈ X is F|_p := F_p ⊗_{O_{X,p}} κ(p).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: O_X|_p is κ(p). Note: this notion will be used later (referenced to later sections). No additional scoring; it's a standard definition with immediate examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compute global sections on unions by intersection of localizations
rubrics_metrics.description: If U = D(x) ∪ D(y) ⊂ Spec k[x,y] (i.e., A^2 minus the origin), then Γ(U, O) equals Ax ∩ Ay inside A_{xy} (or k(x,y)), and in this example the intersection is k[x,y], so removing the origin gives no new regular functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: compute sections on each distinguished open (localizations) and glue by taking intersection inside a common localization/fraction field. Exercise: show Ax ∩ Ay = A in this case; this is how to prove Γ(U,O)=k[x,y].

rubrics_metrics.name: Hartogs-type extension principle in algebraic geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: Any regular function on the complement of a closed subset of codimension ≥ 2 extends across that subset in the normal (or mild singular) case — an algebraic analogue of Hartogs' Lemma.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal remark here; to be made precise later (Theorem 11.3.10). Use this to explain why functions on A^2 minus a point extend to all of A^2. Helpful for anticipating extension results on projective space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for non-affineness via global sections
rubrics_metrics.description: If an open subscheme U were affine, U ≅ Spec A' for A' = Γ(U, O), then the bijection between primes and points would force recovery of closed sets corresponding to ideals; failure to recover expected points/closed sets shows non-affineness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: A^2 \\ {(0,0)} is not affine because Γ(U,O)=k[x,y] but the missing prime (x,y) would have to correspond to a point in Spec k[x,y], contradiction. Use global sections to test affineness and look for primes whose V(I) behavior changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gluing schemes from pieces with cocycle-compatible isomorphisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Given schemes Xi and open subschemes X_{ij} with isomorphisms f_{ij}: X_{ij} → X_{ji} satisfying the cocycle condition (f_{ii}=id and f_{ik}|_{overlap} = f_{jk} ∘ f_{ij} on triple overlaps), there exists a unique scheme X obtained by gluing the Xi along these identifications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construction parallels topological gluing but includes gluing of structure sheaves (see Exercise 2.7.D). Hint: describe X as a quotient set with topology and determine sections on open sets via compatible data. This is the standard gluing lemma for schemes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doubled-origin example and separatedness motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Gluing two copies of A^1 along D(t) ≅ D(1/u) via t ↔ u can produce the affine line with a doubled origin, a non-affine pathological example motivating the notion of separatedness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret this as an analog of failure of Hausdorff-ness; separatedness (to be defined later) prevents such pathologies and ensures intersections of affine opens are affine (Proposition 10.1.8). Exercise: show the doubled-origin scheme is not affine by computing global sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Construction of P^1 by gluing two affines
rubrics_metrics.description: P^1_k is obtained by gluing two copies of A^1 along D(t) ≅ D(u) via the isomorphism t ↔ 1/u. Points glue so that 'a on the t-line' is identified with '1/a on the u-line' (for a≠0), and the generic points glue together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If k is algebraically closed, closed points correspond to [a,b] homogeneous coordinates as usual. Use this to visualize projective gluing; exercise: compute Γ(P^1,O)=k by analyzing polynomials on patches that agree on overlaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Global regular functions on projective space are constants
rubrics_metrics.description: For projective space P^n_k (n>0), Γ(P^n_k, O) ≅ k — the only global regular functions are the constants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof idea: sections on two standard opens must be polynomials that are simultaneously polynomials in coordinates and their inverses, forcing constants. This is an algebraic analogue of the fact holomorphic functions on CP^1 are constant. Exercise 4.4.E generalizes the argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of projective n-space by patches
rubrics_metrics.description: Projective n-space P^n_k can be constructed by gluing n+1 affines U_i ≅ Spec k[x0/i,...,xn/i]/(xi/i − 1), with specified identifications on overlaps via x_k/i = x_k/j / (x_j/i).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This patchwise construction yields the classical coordinate charts; check triple-overlap compatibility (Exercise 4.4.D). Later this is reinterpreted as Proj k[x0,...,xn].

rubrics_metrics.name: Z-graded (and Z_{≥0}-graded) ring and homogeneous elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A Z-graded ring S• = ⊕_{n∈Z} S_n satisfies S_m · S_n ⊂ S_{m+n}. Elements of S_n are homogeneous of degree n. For the book, 'graded ring' means Z_{≥0}-graded unless stated otherwise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: S_0 is a subring, each S_n an S_0-module. Homogeneous ideals are ideals generated by homogeneous elements. Warning: convention (graded ring = nonnegative grading) is nonstandard but used throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization and closure properties of homogeneous ideals
rubrics_metrics.description: An ideal I of a graded ring is homogeneous iff it contains the degree-n piece of each of its elements; homogeneous ideals are closed under sum, product, intersection and radical; primality of homogeneous ideals characterized homogeneously (see Exercise 4.5.C).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use decomposition into homogeneous pieces to test homogeneity. If T is a multiplicative subset of homogeneous elements, T^{-1}S• inherits a grading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Irrelevant ideal S+ and finite generation in graded context
rubrics_metrics.description: S_+ := ⊕_{i>0} S_i is the irrelevant ideal. If S_+ is finitely generated as an ideal, S• is a finitely generated graded ring over A = S_0. If S• is generated by S_1 over A, it is 'generated in degree 1'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: S+ being 'irrelevant' means ideals whose radical contains S+ are geometrically empty in Proj. Exercises relate finite generation of S_+ to Noetherian properties of S•.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proj construction via affine pieces ((S_f)_0)
rubrics_metrics.description: For S• a Z_{≥0}-graded ring and homogeneous f ∈ S_+, consider ((S•)_f)_0, the degree-0 part of the localization at f. The affine pieces of Proj S• are Spec(((S•)_f)_0); Proj S• is obtained by gluing these as f varies over homogeneous elements of positive degree.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motivation: for S•=A[x0,...,xn], taking f=xi recovers the standard affine chart rings. One can either build Proj by gluing these affines or proceed via the homogeneous-prime description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Points of Proj: homogeneous prime ideals not containing S+
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying set of Proj S• is the set of homogeneous prime ideals of S• that do not contain the irrelevant ideal S_+ (i.e., the 'relevant' homogeneous primes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This description helps visualize projective varieties as cones in Spec S• modulo scaling; examples: homogeneous prime (z^2 − x^2 − y^2) corresponds to a conic at infinity in Proj.

rubrics_metrics.name: Projective distinguished opens D(f) and vanishing sets V(T)
rubrics_metrics.description: For homogeneous f of positive degree, define V(f) ⊂ Proj S• as homogeneous primes containing f but not S_+. Let D(f) = Proj S• \, V(f). For a subset T of homogeneous elements, V(T) is primes containing T (but not S_+).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The D(f) form a basis of the Zariski topology on Proj (Exercise 4.5.G). Also D(f) ∩ D(g) = D(fg); stick to positive-degree homogeneous f to ensure affineness of D(f).

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence of primes between ((S_f)_0) and homogeneous primes of (S_f)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a bijection between the primes of ((S•)_f)_0 and the homogeneous prime ideals of (S•)_f (equivalently, homogeneous primes of S• not containing f).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This technical identification (Exercise 4.5.E) underlies the fact that D(f) is 'the same as' Spec(((S•)_f)_0). Use as the key step in showing the local affineness for the Proj topology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characterization of empty vanishing sets and irrelevance of S+
rubrics_metrics.description: For a homogeneous ideal I ⊂ S• contained in S_+, V(I) = ∅ iff the radical √I contains S_+. Equivalently, D(f_i) cover Proj S• for generators f_i of I.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: any ideal whose radical contains S_+ is 'geometrically irrelevant' for Proj. Exercise 4.5.I formalizes these equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure sheaf on Proj and gluing of the affine pieces
rubrics_metrics.description: On each basic open D(f) we define O_{Proj S•}|_{D(f)} to be the structure sheaf of Spec(((S•)_f)_0); these sheaves glue (via the identifications of overlapping Specs) to give the structure sheaf of Proj S•.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises 4.5.K–4.5.L supply the required isomorphisms on overlaps and the triple-overlap checks (Exercise 2.7.D). (Re)interpretation in terms of compatible stalks is Exercise 4.5.M.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of projective and quasiprojective schemes
rubrics_metrics.description: A projective A-scheme is a scheme isomorphic to Proj S• where S• is a finitely generated graded ring over A. A quasiprojective A-scheme is a quasi-compact open subscheme of a projective A-scheme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'A' can often be omitted when clear. In the Noetherian case the quasicompact requirement is redundant. Examples: Proj A[x0,...,xn] = P^n_A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vanishing scheme V(f) as a closed subscheme of Proj when S• generated in degree 1
rubrics_metrics.description: If S• is generated in degree 1 and f ∈ S_+ is homogeneous, one can define a closed subscheme V(f) 'in' Proj S• (even though f is not globally a function on Proj); more generally define V(I) for homogeneous ideals I ⊂ S_+.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning: f is not a global function on Proj in general; one later interprets f as a section of a line bundle (see 14.1.2). Exercise 4.5.P outlines a construction when S• is generated in degree 1; Exercise 13.1.I gives a more general solution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem as geometric decomposition of Spec Z/(n)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spec Z/(60) decomposes into closed points corresponding to the primes dividing 60, with stalks Z/4, Z/3, Z/5; global sections correspond to the product ring Z/4 × Z/3 × Z/5 via the natural map.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Geometric picture: Spec Z/(60) is discrete with closed points [(2)],[(3)],[(5)], and global sections equal the tuple of local sections at each point. Use this to see CRT as a statement about global sections on a scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Example of a section glued from local descriptions lacking a single rational expression
rubrics_metrics.description: There exist sections on an open cover that agree on overlaps yet cannot be written globally as a single rational expression f/g; e.g., on X: wz−xy=0, the local functions z/y on D(y) and x/w on D(w) glue to a section on D(y) ∪ D(w) but have no single global description as an element f/g in k[w,x,y,z].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is analogous to analytic continuation: a function may be described differently on different pieces. The reason here is geometric: the would-be denominator must vanish on a locus not set-theoretically cut out by a single equation. Use this as a caution against assuming global rational expressions always exist for glued sections.
